title: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)
hookLine: one who was careless and becomes earnest lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds
last: REAL FOR A MOMENT, NEVER SOLID.

lines: THREE GOOD WEEKS, THEN TEN DAYS.
STARTING AGAIN IS THE HARD PART.
cards: Three weeks of sitting every morning. Then a trip, a cold, a hard week, and suddenly it's been ten days. Here's the odd part: the stopping was easy.
It's starting again that's hard, because starting again means admitting you stopped, and that can feel embarrassing enough that some people simply never do.
Even the moon disappears for a while behind clouds, and nobody thinks less of it when it comes back.

teach.b: Verse one seventy-two, in Max Müller's translation: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds."
Reckless here means heedless, careless, the opposite of the earnestness from chapter two. The verse doesn't say the careless past vanishes. It says the person, now awake, gives light.
Verse one seventy-three goes further: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds."

The old commentary attaches this verse to a turnaround the early texts tell in full: Aṅgulimāla, the bandit who wore a garland of his victims' fingers, who met the Buddha, stopped, became a monk, and was remembered as having reached awakening.
If the moon can come out from behind that cloud, the story seems to ask, which cloud is too thick?
The Pali word for moon here is candimā, and the picture is simple: the moon sliding free of a cloud, and suddenly you can see the road.

The chapter ends with a striking claim, verse one seventy-eight: "Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all worlds, is the reward of the first step in holiness."
The first step: in the tradition, the moment one first truly enters the stream of the path.
Not the finish line. The first step, and the second beginning, and the third.

how: Buddhist teachers often point to Aṅgulimāla's story and these verses to encourage people to begin again after lapses, and lay Buddhists retake the precepts regularly as a fresh start.

o: a lamp lit at a shrine at night
the moon, sliding free of a cloud
the morning sun after a dark night

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.

s: the verse says the careless past simply vanishes
it says the person, now awake, brightens the world, like the moon freed from clouds.
the commentary links verse 173 to Aṅgulimāla
the bandit who became a monk is the verse's great example.
verse 178 prizes ruling the whole earth above the first step on the path
the reward of the first step is better than sovereignty over the earth.

games.q: you're Aṅgulimāla. you've done terrible harm, and now you've met the Buddha and stopped. what does verse 173 say is possible?
o: good deeds can cover the harm, and you can brighten the world.
forget the past and carry on as before.
games.why: "he whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world." tradition remembers Aṅgulimāla reaching awakening.

practice: Think of one practice you've let slip, sitting, a precept, a kindness you used to do, exercise, a call you used to make, and notice any little cloud of embarrassment around it, without pushing it away.
Picture the moon behind a thin cloud, and the cloud slowly drifting on. Then begin again, right now, in the smallest way: this breath counts, this sit counts.

wordCard.voice: Candimā. The Pali word for the moon: one who was careless and then became earnest lights up the world, like the moon freed from clouds.

orig.note: Pali: the moon — in verses 172–173, the moon freed from a cloud.

carryVoice: Your line: the moon comes out. Beginning again needs no apology and no ceremony. That's day one hundred ninety-two.
